units.title: The hat above the coat
units.instruction: Read the whole story. Choose True or False for each sentence.

materials.title: The hat above the coat
materials.text: Ella wears a red wool hat to school on a cold day. She puts it on the shelf above her coat before the lesson. At home time, she takes her coat but forgets the hat. Outside, the wind makes her ears cold. She asks the teacher if she may go back with an adult. They find the hat exactly where she left it. A small blue glove is beside it, but the glove is not hers. Ella leaves that glove for its owner and puts on her own hat. The teacher suggests checking the shelf before leaving tomorrow. Ella adds a little hat drawing to her bag tag as a reminder.

questions.explanation: The opening gives the colour.

questions.prompt: She puts the hat under her desk.
questions.explanation: It is on a shelf above her coat.

questions.prompt: She remembers the hat before going outside.
questions.explanation: Cold ears outside remind her.

questions.prompt: The blue glove belongs to Ella.
questions.explanation: The text explicitly says it is not hers.

questions.prompt: Ella makes a small reminder drawing.
questions.explanation: She adds a hat drawing to the bag tag.

units.title: The tickets in the yellow envelope
units.instruction: Read the whole story. Choose True or False for each sentence.

materials.title: The tickets in the yellow envelope
materials.text: Tom’s family is going to a puppet show. Mum puts three tickets in a yellow envelope and places it beside her bag. Tom thinks the empty envelope is for drawing, but Mum stops him before he writes on it. She shows him the tickets and explains why they need to keep them together. Tom makes a picture on a different sheet instead. At the theatre, Mum takes the envelope from her bag and gives the tickets to the person at the entrance. Tom keeps his drawing until they are seated. It shows a rabbit puppet with very long ears. The real rabbit on stage has a tiny blue hat.

questions.prompt: There are three tickets in the envelope.
questions.explanation: Three tickets are explicitly counted.
It is yellow.

questions.prompt: Tom writes on the ticket envelope.
questions.explanation: Mum stops him before writing.
He uses different paper for the picture.

questions.prompt: The stage rabbit wears a blue hat.
questions.explanation: The final sentence gives that detail.

units.title: A tiny stage for two dolls
units.instruction: Read the whole story. Choose True or False for each sentence.

materials.title: A tiny stage for two dolls
materials.text: Nora makes a stage from an empty shoe box. She stands it on its side, with the open part facing her. Her brother draws a red curtain on paper and helps fix it around the opening. Two small dolls stand inside. At first, the taller doll touches the top of the box. Nora moves it to the front, where it can stand without bending. She does not cut the doll. They tell a short story about two friends looking for a lost button. A white bead becomes the button in their play. When the story ends, the dolls and bead go into a separate small bag so they will not be lost.

questions.prompt: The stage is made from a shoe box.
questions.explanation: The first sentence identifies the material.
Her brother draws a red curtain.

questions.prompt: Nora cuts the tall doll to make it fit.
questions.explanation: She moves it and explicitly does not cut it.

questions.prompt: A white bead is used as the lost button.
questions.explanation: The bead plays the button in their story.

questions.prompt: They leave the dolls and bead loose on the floor.
questions.explanation: They put them in a separate bag.

units.title: A postcard printed on both sides
units.instruction: Read the whole passage. Use each word at most once. Five words are not needed.

materials.title: A postcard printed on both sides
materials.text:
A postcard combines a picture with space for a message and an address. Designing its two sides requires attention to their different ____1____. A beautiful image does not help a card reach its destination if the address area is unreadable.

The front and back need the correct ____2____ rather than one being upside down relative to the other. A file can look correct on a screen while the reverse side prints in an unexpected direction. A physical proof makes that relationship easier to inspect.

The card's ____3____ affects the result too. A surface that reproduces colour well may not be equally suitable for handwriting. The message area needs to work with the tools people are likely to use.

Enough ____4____ should be left around essential information. Placing small words very close to a cut edge risks losing them or making the layout appear uneven. Trimming has practical tolerances rather than perfect mathematical certainty.

The designer can ____5____ a proof before committing to a large quantity. This is a test of the whole object, including size, colour, orientation and writing space. Looking at only one side leaves important questions unanswered.

A sample also makes an abstract choice ____6____. Someone can hold the card, turn it over and try writing a short line. The test does not reproduce every later use, but it reveals problems a flat preview may hide.

Useful feedback names a particular ____7____, such as a line too small to read. It is more actionable than simply calling the card attractive or unattractive. The designer can then make a targeted ____8____.

Good printing work joins visual judgement with practical checking. The final card should ____9____ its picture and message without forcing the user to solve the layout. A successful design supports the ordinary activity ____10____, even when the decisions behind that ease were quite careful.

questions.explanation: Functions are the two sides’ different jobs.
Orientation names the relative direction of the front and back.
Material is the card surface that affects printing and writing.
Space around essential information protects it from trimming.
Inspect means examine the proof as a whole object.
Tangible means physically available to handling and testing.
Problem identifies a specific issue that can be addressed.
Adjustment is a targeted change to the design.
Present means display or communicate the image and text.
Smoothly describes easy ordinary use; silently concerns sound, not usability.

units.title: What an unnamed response can reveal
units.instruction: Read the whole passage. Use each word at most once. Five words are not needed.

materials.title: What an unnamed response can reveal
materials.text:
Removing a name from a survey response can reduce direct identification, but it does not make the remaining information automatically ____1____. A combination of ordinary details may still point to one person within a small group.

The relevant ____2____ depends on context. A job title that is common across a country may be unique within one office. Reporting it together with an unusual event can make an unnamed account easier to recognise.

Researchers should therefore ____3____ the proposed output rather than consider the name field alone. The question is what a reader could reasonably infer from the information being shared, including combinations across different tables or quotations.

This does not mean all detail must disappear. Removing every meaningful feature can destroy the account's ____4____. The task is to balance useful description with the responsibilities attached to the data and the permission under which it was collected.

A clear plan states which material will be published and at what level of ____5____. Grouped results may serve one purpose while a detailed individual quotation serves another. Neither should be treated as a neutral default without considering the setting.

Participants need an ____6____ of these arrangements. Promising more protection than the process can provide prevents an informed decision. A careful explanation names the actual safeguards and relevant limits.

The team can ____7____ unnecessary identifying details before release, while checking that changes do not distort the substance. Review should focus on plausible risks in the intended audience, not on an abstract claim that identification is either always possible or always impossible.

The final account remains a considered ____8____ rather than a magic property created by deleting one column. Its credibility depends on what was done and whether the description is ____9____. Responsible reporting makes the relationship between detail, permission and protection available for ____10____.

questions.explanation: Anonymous is the claimed non-identification property; names alone do not establish it.
Risk depends on how details identify people in context.
Review means examine the full planned output.
Value is useful substantive information that indiscriminate deletion can remove.
Level of detail is the degree of specificity shared.
An explanation names and makes the arrangements understandable; adjectives do not fit this noun slot.
Remove takes unnecessary details out of the release.
Judgement is a considered decision rather than an automatic property.
Honest describes truthful reporting of the actual arrangement.
Scrutiny is examination of the reporting choices and their basis.

units.title: The ticket kept after the journey
units.instruction: Read the complete passage. Write ONE word in each gap. Gap 0 is an example. Use capital letters; marking ignores case.
units.alignmentNote: Complete original eight-gap, one-word open cloze with fixed example 0. Recorded C1 sample is a task-format reference only; no C1 equivalence or independent learner calibration claimed.

materials.title: The ticket kept after the journey
materials.text:
A ticket stub (0) IS a small object that may outlast the event it once admitted someone to. It can be kept not only for the printed information, ____1____ also for the memory attached to it. A date and seat number become part of a personal account.

There is little point ____2____ assuming that every saved ticket carries the same meaning. One person may remember the performance; another the companion who came along. The object does not speak ____3____ itself without some account of the person who kept it.

A collection can preserve that account as ____4____ as the physical item. A short note about why it was saved may help a later reader understand more than the admission details alone. The note should still distinguish remembered experience from what the ticket itself establishes.

No matter ____5____ vivid a memory feels, the printed date and the remembered sequence can disagree. Such a difference need not make the object or the person worthless as a source. It gives the reader a question to examine.

To some ____6____, an ordinary keepsake has two histories: its original practical role and its later life as a reminder. As ____7____ as those roles are kept clear, both can be described without forcing them into one story. The small piece of paper remains open ____8____ further interpretation rather than carrying a complete life inside its edges.

questions.explanation: Not only ... but also is the pair.
Little point in assuming uses in.
Speak for itself is the expression.
As well as adds the physical item.
No matter how vivid uses how with the adjective.
To some extent/degree limits the claim.
As long as introduces a condition.
Open to interpretation takes to.

materials.title: The name given to a footpath
materials.text:
A familiar footpath (0) MAY have one name on a public map and another among people who use it daily. The difference does not necessarily mean that one group is wrong. It may reflect a distinction ____1____ an official label and a local habit.

There is no point ____2____ recording only the printed name if the project aims to understand how residents describe their journeys. Equally, a guide for new visitors needs to make the relation to official signs clear.

The record can preserve more ____3____ one name, provided it explains who used each and in what setting. A local phrase should not automatically be presented as though everyone in the area agreed ____4____ it.

No matter ____5____ familiar a name seems to one contributor, another may never have heard it. Asking a wider question can reveal that variation without making the first speaker's experience disappear.

The writer can distinguish quotation from summary as ____6____ as keep the date of the account. That helps a later reader see whether the wording records one person's usage or the project's own description. As ____7____ as the distinction remains visible, a modest list can support further inquiry. It becomes useful not by claiming to speak on ____8____ of the whole community, but by showing the basis of each entry.

questions.explanation: Between two naming practices expresses the distinction.
No point in recording uses in.
More than one uses comparative than.
Agree on/about a name are both appropriate prepositions.
No matter how familiar uses how.
As well as is additive.
As long as sets the condition.
Speak on behalf of is the expression.
